name: Chronotype Test
tagline: Morning person or night owl? Find your natural daily rhythm.
intro: This test looks at your chronotype: when in the day you feel most alert, when your body wants to sleep and wake, and how easily you adapt when your schedule changes. Answer based on what feels natural to you, especially on days when you can choose your own hours. It takes about five minutes and gives you concrete advice on the best times for focus, exercise and sleep.
seoTitle: Chronotype Test – Are you a morning person or night owl?
seoDescription: Early bird or night owl? Take this free 5-minute chronotype test and get personal advice on the best hours for focus work, exercise and sleep.

morning_alertness.name: Morning alertness
morning_alertness.short: How awake, sharp and energetic you feel in the early part of the day.
morning_alertness.low: Your answers suggest mornings are not your strongest time. You may need a while to warm up, and complex thinking feels harder before mid-morning. Where you can, keep the first hour for routine tasks such as email or planning, and schedule focus work from late morning onwards. Bright daylight soon after waking, a short walk and a proper breakfast can help you feel awake sooner. Avoid booking important meetings or exams early when you have a choice.
morning_alertness.mid: You can function reasonably well in the morning, though you may not be at your absolute peak right after waking. Most people with this pattern find their sharpest window between roughly 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Use that slot for your most demanding work and save lighter tasks for the very start of the day. Getting outdoor light within an hour of waking helps stabilise your rhythm, and a consistent wake-up time keeps your mornings predictable.
morning_alertness.high: Your answers point to strong early-bird traits. You feel alert soon after waking and do your best thinking in the first half of the day. Protect roughly 7 to 11 a.m. for deep focus work and hard decisions, and consider exercising early when your energy is high. Schedule routine tasks and meetings for the afternoon. Remember that your energy may dip earlier in the evening, so avoid saving important tasks for late in the day. If you find yourself waking far too early and feeling unrested, a doctor or qualified sleep professional can help.

evening_alertness.name: Evening alertness
evening_alertness.short: How awake, focused and energetic you feel later in the day and at night.
evening_alertness.low: Your energy tends to fade as the evening goes on. Late nights cost you more than they give, and focus is hard after dinner. Plan demanding work earlier in the day and keep evenings for calm activities such as reading, light social time or a walk. Avoid intense workouts or screens close to bedtime, as they can make winding down harder. Respecting this early dip will usually improve both your sleep and your mood the next day.
evening_alertness.mid: You can be productive in the evening, but you do not rely on it. Your energy may hold steady into the early evening and then gradually decline. A good rhythm for you is focus work in late morning or early afternoon and lighter tasks after 6 p.m. Exercise in the late afternoon often works well. Try to keep a regular cut-off for screens and work, so a pleasant second wind does not push your bedtime later than you intended.
evening_alertness.high: Your answers point to strong night-owl traits. You come alive later in the day and may do your best thinking in the evening. Where your life allows it, schedule focus work from mid-afternoon into the evening and exercise in the late afternoon or early evening. Keep mornings light. To avoid chronic sleep loss, aim for a fixed wake-up time, get daylight early and dim lights an hour before bed. If a late rhythm clashes with work or school and affects your wellbeing, a doctor or qualified sleep professional can help.

sleep_timing.name: Sleep timing
sleep_timing.short: How early your body naturally wants to fall asleep and wake up.
sleep_timing.low: Your natural sleep window seems to be on the late side. Your body may prefer falling asleep after midnight and waking later in the morning, which can clash with early schedules. Try to keep your wake-up time consistent, even at weekends, and get bright light soon after waking to nudge your clock earlier. In the evening, dim lights and limit screens for the last hour. Small shifts of 15 minutes every few days work better than big jumps.
sleep_timing.mid: Your sleep timing sits in the middle range. You probably feel most natural falling asleep somewhere between 11 p.m. and midnight and waking between 7 and 8 a.m. This fits many work and school schedules reasonably well. Keep your rhythm stable by going to bed and getting up at similar times every day. If you notice weekends drifting much later, try limiting lie-ins to about an hour so Monday mornings feel less heavy.
sleep_timing.high: Your body seems to favour an early sleep window. You likely get sleepy well before midnight and wake early, even without an alarm. Embrace this by keeping a regular bedtime around 9:30 to 10:30 p.m. and using your early hours for focused or creative work. Late social plans may cost you more, so plan them sparingly and protect your sleep afterwards. If you keep waking much earlier than you want and feel tired during the day, a doctor or qualified sleep professional can help.

flexibility.name: Flexibility
flexibility.short: How easily you adapt to shifted schedules, travel and irregular hours.
flexibility.low: Your answers suggest your body likes routine. Changes in sleep times, travel or late nights can leave you drained for a while. Protect a consistent bedtime and wake-up time as much as possible. Before trips or schedule changes, shift your sleep by 15 to 30 minutes a day in advance. Afterwards, get daylight at the right time and allow yourself extra recovery. Knowing this about yourself helps you plan demanding events with enough buffer.
flexibility.mid: You adapt reasonably well to changes in your schedule, but bigger shifts still take some time to recover from. An occasional late night or early flight is manageable, especially if you plan for it. Keep your anchor habits, such as a regular wake-up time and morning light, stable even when other parts of your day change. After a disruption, return to your normal rhythm quickly instead of sleeping in for several days.
flexibility.high: Your body seems to adapt easily to shifted schedules, travel and irregular hours. This is a real advantage for shift work, travel or busy social lives. Still, flexibility does not mean you need less sleep overall. Keep track of your total hours and make sure recovery nights happen after short ones. Use your adaptability wisely: you can move workouts or focus blocks to suit the day. If irregular hours start affecting your mood or health, a doctor or qualified professional can help you review your routine.

summary: Your chronotype is your body's natural timing preference. Below you see four scores from 0 to 100 %: how alert you feel in the morning, how alert you feel in the evening, how early your natural sleep window is and how easily you adapt to shifted schedules. Read them together to find your ideal daily rhythm. This report is based on your own answers and is not a medical sleep assessment.
